title: Where output goes
summary: stdin, stdout and stderr: send output to a file, keep the errors apart, or throw them away.

text: Every program starts with three streams, each with a number:
- stdin (0): what it reads, the keyboard by default.
- stdout (1): its normal output, the results.
Both outputs go to your screen, so they look the same. They are not.
> sends stdout into a file. The errors still show on the screen.
- > empties the file first! Every run replaces it.
- >> adds at the end of the file instead: good for a log.
2> sends stream number 2, the errors, somewhere else.
- Results in one file, problems in another: easy to read later.
- 2> /dev/null throws the errors away. /dev/null is a bin that swallows everything.
2>&1 means: send 2 to the same place as 1, right now.
- Order matters: first > all.log, then 2>&1. The other way round, the errors still go to the screen.
- Useful for cron jobs and scripts: the whole story ends up in one file.
< does the opposite: the program reads a file as if you were typing it.
- Most tools also take the file name as an argument: sort names.txt.
- < matters for programs that only read stdin, like a script waiting for your answers.
